newsitem.title: FRANCE: Some railmen strike as French Senate weighs reform.
newsitem.headline: Some railmen strike as French Senate weighs reform.

text.p: France's SNCF state railways said a 24-hour strike had no impact on Tuesday, while a rail reform bill opposed by two large trade unions started its passage through parliament.
An SNCF spokesman said there was "no disruption at all" from a strike called by the SUD-Rail union, which represents a small number of railway staff.

The more threatening opponents of the railways reform bill, which involves setting up a separate state company as owner of the infrastructure, are the Communist-led CGT and the Socialist CFDT, the latter of which is planning a strike on January 31.

Meanwhile, Transport Minister Bernard Pons presented his bill to the Senate on the first day of a three-day examination in the upper house of parliament and reiterated declarations that the reform in no way entailed a break-up of the SNCF.

"Contrary to what is sometimes claimed, there will of course be no dismantling of the SNCF. The new state company will be a tiny structure with 200 staff, while, I remind you, the SNCF accounts for nearly 180,000," Pons told the Senate.

The state company which would become owner of the network under the Pons plan would also take over 134.2 billion francs of the SNCF's debts, which total 208 billion francs and were mainly run up developing France's high-speed TGV train system.
The new company, likely to be called France Rail, would charge the SNCF fees for using the network.

The CFDT argues that the plan amounts to a split which could be a precursor to opening France's railways to competition, but although the Communist-led CGT takes a similar line, it has not joined the CFDT strike and says it is assessing its options.
The CGT and CFDT are the largest and second largest unions within the SNCF respectively.

France was crippled by a railway strike at the end of 1995 but the government has since dropped the proposals which sparked the trouble, primarily an attack SNCF staff's right to retire earlier than the standard 60 years of age.
Pons had also backed down temporarily on the latest reform, when he decided in November to put the bill on hold in the face of union disquiet.

But he has now revived the bill after raising the amount of debt taken off SNCF hands from 125 billion to 134.2 billion francs and subsequently winning backing from a majority of the unions in the railway company.
